passage: The power was out and the lift was dead, so Aadhya carried her son Yash, four, up six flights while the neighbours' generator hummed. The cough syrup was already on the spoon. Yash pressed his lips tight, and turned his face away, gripping the banister. "Open up, Yash," said Aadhya, her arms aching. She stopped and breathed. "Do you want the red spoon or the blue cup?" He looked at both, then at her, and reached for the blue cup, mouth still shut. Then he opened it.

qa.q: How many flights of stairs did Aadhya carry Yash up?
qa.a: She carried him up six flights.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when he pressed his lips tight, and what else might it mean?
qa.a: He was probably determined to keep some control over what went into his mouth, since he turned away and gripped the banister. He might also have been reluctant because he disliked the taste.

qa.q: What did Aadhya do that worked better than insisting?
qa.a: She offered a limited choice between the red spoon and the blue cup, so Yash had some say.

qa.q: How might Aadhya be feeling as she stands on the stairs with the spoon?
qa.a: She is likely tired and a little frustrated, since her arms were aching, yet she paused and breathed instead of forcing him.

grounding: A preschooler presses his lips shut to refuse medicine, wanting control, and a limited choice works better than force.

passage:
At the dining table in their Nagpur flat, Ojas pressed his lips together and shook his head at the spinach on his spoon.
"Just one bite," said Harish.
"No." It came out through closed teeth.
"Okay. Spinach on the plate or in the roti roll?"
Ojas thought. "Roll."
"Then you fold it."
Ojas folded it carefully, lips still tight, then bit down and chewed. "Tastes okay," he said, sounding surprised.

qa.q: What did Ojas choose to have his spinach in?
qa.a: He chose to have it in the roti roll.

qa.q: What did Ojas want when he pressed his lips together?
qa.a: He seems to have wanted a say in what he ate, because he accepted the spinach once he could choose how it came and fold it himself. It might also have been dislike of the look of it.

qa.q: What could Harish try the next time Ojas refuses food?
qa.a: He could offer two acceptable choices again and let Ojas take part in preparing his food.

qa.q: How might Harish feel when Ojas bites the roll and says it tastes okay?
qa.a: Harish may feel relieved and pleased that offering a choice worked, since Ojas ate the spinach without a fight.

grounding: A preschooler presses his lips to refuse food, and a limited choice restores his sense of control.

passage:
“Rajni, cough medicine time.”
Rajni pressed her lips into a tight line and shook her head.
“It tastes bad, I know,” said Sangeeta. “But the doctor gave it to help your cough.”
Rajni's lips stayed shut. She hid behind the curtain.
“Okay. You choose. The spoon or the little cup?”
A pause. “…Cup.”
“And before your story or after?”
“Before. Then story.”
“Deal.” Sangeeta held out the little cup. Rajni took it herself, made a face, and swallowed. “Now two stories,” she bargained.

qa.q: What did Rajni choose to take her medicine from?
qa.a: The little cup.

qa.q: What did Rajni's tight lips and hiding behind the curtain suggest she wanted?
qa.a: She probably disliked the taste and wanted some control over what happened to her, feeling cross at being told. She may also have been a bit scared of the bad taste.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Offering a limited choice, spoon or cup and before or after the story, gave Rajni control over how, while the medicine still happened.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel if she had forced the spoon in?
qa.a: She would likely feel stressed and guilty, and the next dose might become an even bigger fight.

grounding: A preschooler presses her lips to refuse medicine, wanting control, and her mother offers a limited choice instead of force.

passage:
Lunch note from Chetan, nursery teacher.
Imran sat down, looked at the dal and pressed his lips shut so hard they went pale. He pushed the bowl away with one finger. I did not push it back. I said, “Would you like to start with the rice, or dip the roti?” He looked at me a long time, then pointed at the roti. He ate three bites of dal with it. I didn't praise the eating, just chatted about his drawing. Tomorrow I'll offer the same small choice again.

qa.q: What did Imran point at when Chetan offered a choice?
qa.a: The roti.

qa.q: What might Imran's pale, pressed lips suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He probably felt stubborn and wanted to be in charge of what went into his mouth, possibly because he didn't like the dal. It could also be that he wasn't hungry yet.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Chetan to chat about the drawing instead of praising the eating?
qa.a: It kept lunch relaxed and did not turn eating into a contest, so Imran was less likely to refuse again to show control.

qa.q: How might Imran's parents see this note?
qa.a: They might feel relieved to learn that a small choice, not pressure, helped him eat, and try the same at home.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a preschooler pressing his lips to refuse food and a limited choice working better than force.

passage: In the courtyard, Dilnaz Khala served karela sabzi to all the children. Jeevan took one look and clamped his lips shut, cheeks puffed, eyes on the goats. The other children laughed. Khala didn't. She sat beside him on the charpai. “You don't have to finish it. Do you want one tiny piece with jaggery roti, or none today and try again at Eid?” Jeevan considered, lips still pressed. Then he opened them just enough to say, “One tiny piece.” He chewed it very slowly.

qa.q: What sabzi did Dilnaz Khala serve?
qa.a: Karela sabzi.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when he clamped his lips shut?
qa.a: He was probably disgusted by the bitter food and embarrassed when the other children laughed. His pressed lips also showed he wanted to decide for himself.

qa.q: How could Khala build on this next time?
qa.a: She could keep offering small, clear choices and let him decide the amount, so tasting new food stays his decision.

qa.q: How might the other children see Jeevan's pressed lips?
qa.a: They saw it as funny, not understanding that Jeevan was uncomfortable and needed a way out without being pushed.

grounding: A child presses his lips shut to refuse a food, and an adult offers a limited choice rather than force.

passage:
In their small kitchen in Kraków, Ivan held out a forkful of green beans. Leila pressed her lips into a tight line and turned her face away.

"Just one bite," Ivan said, moving the fork closer. Her lips squeezed even tighter, and she slid down in her chair.

Ivan put the fork down and thought for a moment. "Okay. Do you want your beans with cheese on top, or dipped in the soup?"

Leila sat up. "Dipped." She took the fork herself and dunked a bean.

qa.q: Where was Ivan's kitchen?
qa.a: In Kraków.

qa.q: What was Leila feeling when she pressed her lips tighter and slid down in her chair?
qa.a: She was likely frustrated and stubborn, wanting some control over what went into her mouth. She may also simply have disliked the taste of green beans.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Offering two small options, cheese on top or dipped in soup, gave Leila a say, so she chose to eat instead of fighting.

qa.q: How might Ivan feel when "just one bite" makes Leila squeeze her lips tighter?
qa.a: He is probably a bit stuck and impatient, which is why he stops and thinks of another way.

grounding: It shows a preschooler pressing her lips shut to refuse food and a limited choice working better than pushing.
